SPREG: Structured Plan Repair with Entropy-Guided Test-Time Intervention for Large Language Model Reasoning

Xuan Wang Affiliation: Meituan Email: 0.8wangxuan39@meituan.com    Yu Ming Affiliation: Meituan Email: mingyu03@meituan.com    Xinhao Zhong Affiliation: Meituan Email: zhongxinhao@meituan.com    Xinyu Yu Affiliation: Meituan Email: yuxinyu08@meituan.com    Wenjie Wang Affiliation: Meituan Email: wangwenjie22@meituan.com    Shuai Chen Affiliation: Meituan Email: chenshuai31@meituan.com    Wei Lin Affiliation: Meituan Email: linwei31@meituan.com
Abstract

Large Language Models (LLMs) are prone to logical hallucinations and stochastic drifts during long-chain reasoning. While Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) can improve instruction adherence, standard static implementations often cause semantic dilution and linguistic degradation. We propose SPREG (Structured Plan-guided Real-time Entropy Gating), a lightweight inference-time framework for surgical error rectification. SPREG employs an adaptive dual-threshold mechanism to monitor real-time entropy, identifying sudden “entropy spikes” as reliable indicators of logical failure. Upon detection, it triggers a dynamic repair by replacing uninformative null-priors with reference distributions synthesized from historical high-confidence states. By modulating guidance intensity according to structured reasoning stages (e.g., Action, Observation), SPREG steers the model back to a stable manifold without compromising fluency. Our experiments demonstrate significant gains, notably a 20.0% absolute accuracy improvement on AIME25, while effectively suppressing uncontrolled entropy drift in complex tasks.

1 Introduction

The paradigm of Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) Sanchez et al. (2024b) has emerged as a powerful technique for enhancing instruction adherence in generative models. By extrapolating conditional logits away from an “unconditional” prior, CFG forces the model to prioritize task-specific constraints. Formally, given a condition cc and the (t+1)(t+1)-th token, the guided log-probability is:

log⁡P^θ​(yt+1|𝐲<t+1,c)=log⁡Pθ​(yt+1|𝐲<t+1)+γ⁡(log⁡Pθ​(yt+1|𝐲<t+1,c)−log⁡Pθ​(yt+1|𝐲<t+1))\begin{split}\log\widehat{\text{P}}_{\theta}(y_{t+1}|\mathbf{y}_{<t+1},c)&=\log\text{P}_{\theta}(y_{t+1}|\mathbf{y}_{<t+1})\\ &\quad+\gamma\left(\log\text{P}_{\theta}(y_{t+1}|\mathbf{y}_{<t+1},c)-\log\text{P}_{\theta}(y_{t+1}|\mathbf{y}_{<t+1})\right)\end{split} (1)

where γ≥1\gamma\geq 1 governs the guidance intensity. Despite its success in image generation, applying static CFG to Large Language Models (LLMs) reveals a critical limitation: Indiscriminate Guidance. Since standard CFG applies a constant γ\gamma to the entire logit vector at every decoding step, it inadvertently suppresses valid semantic candidates and introduces distribution shifts that degrade linguistic fluency Sanchez et al. (2024b); Yang et al. (2025b). This over-correction is particularly damaging in complex reasoning, where the null prior fails to account for the evolving logical dependencies of the reasoning chain.

We argue that the key to robust reasoning lies in state-aware adaptive intervention Dong et al. (2025). Our preliminary analysis shows that the predictive entropy HtH_{t} of LLMs provides a high-fidelity signal of internal hesitation. As illustrated in Figure 1, logical inconsistencies and the onset of hallucinations are preceded by sudden “Entropy Spikes.” These spikes indicate that the model’s autoregressive trajectory has entered a region of high epistemic uncertainty, necessitating immediate rectification.

To bridge this gap, we propose SPREG (Structured Plan-guided Real-time Entropy Gating), an inference-time framework that transforms CFG from a static constraint into a dynamic repair mechanism. SPREG employs an adaptive thresholding scheme to monitor entropy fluctuations in real time, triggering intervention only when a spike is detected. Crucially, SPREG replaces the uninformative null prior with a Dynamic Reference Distribution derived from the model’s own low-entropy historical states. By selectively sharpening the output distribution at points of failure, SPREG steers the model back toward a high-confidence reasoning path without the semantic dilution associated with traditional CFG. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We characterize the entropy dynamics of LLMs during structured reasoning and identify entropy spikes as a reliable leading indicator of logical hallucinations.

  • •

    We propose SPREG, an inference-time framework that combines plan-guided gating with an adaptive CFG mechanism for surgical error rectification.

  • •

    We demonstrate that SPREG significantly enhances the accuracy of reasoning on challenging benchmarks (e.g. + 20.0% on AIME25) while preserving linguistic integrity.

2 Related Work

Classifier-Free Guidance for Language Models.

CFG was originally proposed for diffusion-based image generation Ho and Salimans (2022), where it steers the denoising trajectory by amplifying the gap between conditional and unconditional score estimates. Recent work has adapted this idea to autoregressive LLMs. Sanchez et al. (2024a) showed that applying CFG at the token level can improve instruction following, while Yang et al. (2025b) demonstrated that reducing guidance on high-confidence tokens mitigates over-suppression of valid continuations. Despite these advances, all existing LLM-CFG methods apply a fixed guidance scale throughout generation, leaving them vulnerable to the indiscriminate guidance problem we identify in this work.

Uncertainty Estimation and Entropy in LLMs.

Predictive entropy has long been used as a proxy for model uncertainty in Bayesian deep learning Gal and Ghahramani (2016). In the context of LLMs, Kadavath et al. (2022) showed that well-calibrated models exhibit higher entropy on questions they are likely to answer incorrectly. Malinin and Gales (2021) studied ensemble-based uncertainty decomposition for sequence models, and Kuhn et al. (2023) proposed semantic entropy as a more robust uncertainty measure for free-form generation. Our work builds on this line of research by treating token-level entropy as a real-time signal for detecting reasoning failures, rather than as a post-hoc evaluation metric.

Inference-Time Scaling and Reasoning.

A growing body of work explores how to improve LLM reasoning at inference time without modifying model weights. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting Wei et al. (2022) elicits multi-step reasoning by conditioning on intermediate steps. Self-consistency Wang et al. (2023) improves reliability by sampling multiple reasoning paths and taking a majority vote. More recent approaches such as Tree-of-Thought Yao et al. (2023a) and Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based methods Zhang et al. (2024) explicitly search over reasoning trajectories. Process Reward Models (PRMs) Lightman et al. (2024) provide step-level supervision to guide search. SPREG is complementary to these approaches: rather than searching over multiple trajectories, it repairs a single trajectory on the fly by detecting and correcting entropy spikes, making it compatible with standard greedy or beam-search decoding.

Hallucination Detection and Mitigation.

Hallucination in LLMs has been studied extensively from both the training and inference perspectives Ji et al. (2023). Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) Lewis et al. (2020) grounds model outputs in external knowledge, while contrastive decoding Li et al. (2023) suppresses outputs that are disproportionately likely under a weaker model. Chuang et al. (2024) proposed DoLa, which contrasts later and earlier layer logits to reduce factual errors. Closest to our work, Dong et al. (2025) explored agentic intervention strategies that monitor internal model states to trigger corrective actions. SPREG differs from these methods in that it uses entropy dynamics—rather than external knowledge or layer-wise contrasts—to identify the precise token positions where hallucinations are imminent, and applies a targeted CFG correction only at those positions.

Structured Reasoning and Plan Tracking.

Several works have explored imposing explicit structure on LLM reasoning chains. Scratchpad methods Nye et al. (2021) encourage models to write intermediate computations, while Zhou et al. (2023) decompose complex problems into ordered sub-problems. In the agentic setting, ReAct Yao et al. (2023b) interleaves reasoning and action steps with structured keywords. SPREG’s PlanTracker component is inspired by this line of work: it identifies step boundaries (reasoning, action, observation, conclusion) via lightweight keyword matching, enabling context-aware guidance that reduces intervention during stable conclusion steps.

3 Methodology

We introduce SPREG (Structured Plan-guided Real-time Entropy Gating), a lightweight framework designed to enhance the reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs) during complex reasoning. As illustrated in Figure 2, SPREG operates via an adaptive “Monitor-Detect-Repair” loop, selectively intervening only when the model’s predictive trajectory exhibits high-uncertainty anomalies.

3.1 Adaptive Detection via Historical Entropy Patterns

To identify potential reasoning failures, SPREG monitors the Shannon entropy HtH_{t} of the predictive distribution PtP_{t} at each decoding step tt:

Ht=−∑v∈Vpt,vlogpt,vH_{t}=-\sum_{v\in V}p_{t,v}\log p_{t,v} (2)

Rather than relying on static thresholds, SPREG maintains a sliding window 𝒲t\mathcal{W}_{t} of size W=10W=10 to estimate the local manifold of model uncertainty.

3.1.1 Dual-Threshold Spike Detection

To distinguish meaningful “hesitation” from inherent linguistic variance, we define an Entropy Spike using a dual-threshold mechanism. An intervention is triggered only if:

is_spike=[Ht>μW+α⋅σW]∧[Ht≥Hmin]\text{is\_spike}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[H_{t}>\mu_{W}+\alpha\cdot\sigma_{W}\right]\wedge\mathbf{1}\!\left[H_{t}\geq H_{\min}\right] (3)

where μW\mu_{W} and σW\sigma_{W} are the moving average and standard deviation within 𝒲t\mathcal{W}_{t}. Motivation: The relative sensitivity α=1.5\alpha=1.5 captures local anomalies, while the absolute floor Hmin=2.0H_{\min}=2.0 filters out stochastic noise in high-confidence regions, ensuring the precision of the trigger.

3.1.2 Gradient-based Pre-filtering

Before triggering the dual-threshold check, we analyze the Entropy Gradient gtg_{t} over the last n=5n=5 steps to estimate the instantaneous rate of uncertainty change:

gt=∑i=0n−1(i−i¯)​(Ht−n+1+i−H¯)∑i=0n−1(i−i¯)2g_{t}=\frac{\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(i-\bar{i})(H_{t-n+1+i}-\bar{H})}{\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(i-\bar{i})^{2}} (4)

where i¯=(n−1)/2\bar{i}=(n-1)/2. If the entropy increases slowly (gt<gmin=0.3g_{t}<g_{\min}=0.3) and remains moderate (Ht<3.5H_{t}<3.5), it is categorized as a natural semantic transition. Only rapid surges (gt≥gming_{t}\geq g_{\min}) or extreme states (Ht≥3.5H_{t}\geq 3.5) are treated as potential failures.

3.1.3 Temporal Intervention Control

To preserve fluency and avoid cumulative bias, SPREG employs a three-phase control rhythm:

  • •

    Warm-up: No detection occurs during the first Twarm=5T_{\text{warm}}=5 steps to allow the entropy window to stabilize.

  • •

    Repair: Upon a trigger, intervention persists for drepair∈{1,2,3}d_{\text{repair}}\in\{1,2,3\} steps (dynamically decided by severity) to stabilize the reasoning path.

  • •

    Cooldown: A period of Tcool=30T_{\text{cool}}=30 steps follows each repair to prevent frequent oscillations and over-correction.

3.2 Entropy-Guided Adaptive Plan Repair

When a spike is detected, SPREG modulates the output distribution using an entropy-aware Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) framework.

3.2.1 Dynamic CFG Formulation

Unlike standard CFG which utilizes a fixed prior, we define guided logits 𝐳~t\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{t} that extrapolate away from a dynamic reference distribution 𝐳tref\mathbf{z}_{t}^{\text{ref}}:

𝐳~t=𝐳tref+λ⁡(Ht,τ,r)⋅𝐰t⊙(𝐳tc−𝐳tref)\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{t}=\mathbf{z}_{t}^{\text{ref}}+\lambda(H_{t},\tau,r)\cdot\mathbf{w}_{t}\odot\left(\mathbf{z}_{t}^{c}-\mathbf{z}_{t}^{\text{ref}}\right) (5)

where 𝐳tc\mathbf{z}_{t}^{c} denotes conditional logits, λ\lambda is the adaptive guidance scale, and 𝐰t\mathbf{w}_{t} is a token-level weight. For numerical stability, the computation is performed in log-softmax space: ℓ~t=λ⁡(ℓtc−ℓtref)+ℓtref\tilde{\ell}_{t}=\lambda(\ell_{t}^{c}-\ell_{t}^{\text{ref}})+\ell_{t}^{\text{ref}}.

3.2.2 Reference Prior and Efficiency

The reference prior 𝐳tref\mathbf{z}_{t}^{\text{ref}} represents the model’s grounded state, synthesized by aggregating historical low-entropy distributions where Hs<μWH_{s}<\mu_{W}. In practice, we approximate this prior via an unconditional forward pass with a neutral prompt. By setting dont_save_kv_cache=True, we reuse the existing KV cache of the conditional prefix without contamination, significantly reducing the computational overhead of the guidance.

3.2.3 Adaptive Guidance Scaling and Token Weighting

The scale λ\lambda is dynamically scaled based on the reasoning step type τ\tau (from Table 1), current entropy, and repair count rr:

λ⁡(Ht,τ,r)=min⁡(λbase​(τ)⋅(1+β​Ht−μWμW+ϵ)⋅γ⁡(τ)⋅δ⁡(r),λmax)\lambda(H_{t},\tau,r)=\min\!\left(\lambda_{\text{base}}(\tau)\cdot\left(1+\beta\frac{H_{t}-\mu_{W}}{\mu_{W}+\epsilon}\right)\cdot\gamma(\tau)\cdot\delta(r),\ \lambda_{\max}\right) (6)

where δ⁡(r)=1/(1+r)\delta(r)=1/(1+r) is a decay factor. Furthermore, we introduce Token-level Weighting 𝐰t\mathbf{w}_{t} based on the reference distribution variance:

𝐰t​(v)=1+η⋅H^t⋅𝐳tref​(v)−μrefσref+ϵ\mathbf{w}_{t}(v)=1+\eta\cdot\hat{H}_{t}\cdot\frac{\mathbf{z}_{t}^{\text{ref}}(v)-\mu_{\text{ref}}}{\sigma_{\text{ref}}+\epsilon} (7)

where H^t=Ht/log⁡|V|\hat{H}_{t}=H_{t}/\log|V| is the normalized entropy. This weighting penalizes anomalous tokens that deviate from the high-confidence mean, providing surgical precision during intervention.

3.2.4 Aggressive Recovery and Loop Detection

In cases of persistent uncertainty (e.g., Chigh≥50C_{\text{high}}\geq 50 consecutive steps above μW\mu_{W}), SPREG activates an Aggressive Recovery Mode. In this state, we amplify λ\lambda, apply a sharp temperature T=0.3T=0.3, and impose a repetition penalty ρ\rho to break logical loops:

z^t​(v)←{z^t​(v)/ρif ​v∈𝒱recent​ and ​z^t​(v)>0z^t​(v)⋅ρif ​v∈𝒱recent​ and ​z^t​(v)<0\hat{z}_{t}(v)\leftarrow\begin{cases}\hat{z}_{t}(v)/\rho&\text{if }v\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{recent}}\text{ and }\hat{z}_{t}(v)>0\\ \hat{z}_{t}(v)\cdot\rho&\text{if }v\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{recent}}\text{ and }\hat{z}_{t}(v)<0\end{cases} (8)

where 𝒱recent\mathcal{V}_{\text{recent}} is the set of tokens generated in the previous window. This forces the model to explore new semantic paths and exit the deterministic error state.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks. We evaluate SPREG on a spectrum of challenging reasoning tasks: (1) Mathematical Reasoning: AIME24Zhang and Math-AI (2024), AIME25Zhang and Math-AI (2025), AMC23, MATH-500, and Minerva; (2) Scientific Reasoning: GPQARein et al. (2024); (3) Comprehensive Benchmarks: Olympiad-BenchHe et al. (2024). These datasets are selected to test the model’s ability to maintain logical consistency over extended reasoning chains.

Implementation Details. Our experiments are conducted using Qwen3-8BYang et al. (2025a) as the base model. The sliding window size for entropy monitoring is set to 𝒲=10\mathcal{W}=10, and the spike sensitivity α\alpha is 2.0. We implement the PlanTracker using highly optimized regular expressions. For the adaptive repair, we set the base guidance scale γbase\gamma_{\text{base}} to 1.51.5 for reasoning steps and 1.81.8 for action/conclusion steps.

4.2 Main Results

Table 2 summarizes the performance. SPREG achieves significant gains on the hardest math competition datasets (AIME24 and AIME25), where precise logical control is paramount. Interestingly, while the overall accuracy gain on larger benchmarks like MATH-500 is marginal, the high volume of Spikes (37,222 in total) underscores the prevalence of uncertainty during reasoning, which SPREG successfully manages without degrading fluency.

4.3 Qualitative Analysis: Entropy Dynamics and Error Rectification

To further understand how SPREG stabilizes reasoning, we analyze the entropy trajectory in Figure 3, yielding several key insights:

  • •

    Proactive Anomaly Detection: The 37,222 total spikes reported in Table 2 highlight the ubiquity of uncertainty in long-chain reasoning. Figure 3 shows that SPREG identifies critical “decision forks” (red arrows) before the model commits to erroneous tokens.

  • •

    Effective Trajectory Control: Unlike the baseline (dashed grey line) which exhibits uncontrolled entropy drift and divergence, SPREG’s intervention (green regions) successfully pulls the entropy back to a stable, low-uncertainty manifold (Ht<1.0H_{t}<1.0).

  • •

    Precision and Robustness: The Hmin=2.0H_{\min}=2.0 floor prevents unnecessary intervention in fluent, low-uncertainty zones. The significant gains on AIME25 (+20.0%) and AIME24 (+6.6%) demonstrate SPREG’s efficacy in high-stakes competition tasks where a single logical slip leads to complete failure.

  • •

    Loop Suppression: SPREG effectively mitigates the upward entropy drift characteristic of circular reasoning or “rambling” observed in the late stages of baseline generation, contributing to the consistent gains on Olympiad-Bench (+0.6%).

  • •

    Limitations of Confidence-Based Guidance: A small number of datasets exhibit marginal performance degradation (GPQA: −1.0%-1.0\%; MATH-500: −0.2%-0.2\%). We attribute this to an inherent limitation of entropy-based intervention: SPREG amplifies the model’s own distributional tendencies, and therefore cannot correct errors that arise from overconfident mispredictions. When the model assigns extremely low entropy to an incorrect reasoning path—i.e., it is confidently wrong —no spike is detected and no repair is triggered. Moreover, by sharpening the distribution at intervention points, SPREG may inadvertently suppress the stochastic diversity that would otherwise allow a correct answer to emerge via random sampling. This effect is most pronounced on datasets such as GPQA, whose questions demand broad world knowledge that may lie outside the model’s reliable competence boundary, making high-confidence errors more frequent. Addressing this limitation, for instance by incorporating external verifiers or process reward signals to detect confident-yet-wrong states, is a promising direction for future work.

5 Conclusion and Future Work

In this paper, we introduced SPREG, a novel inference-time framework that enhances the logical consistency of LLMs through structured plan-guided entropy monitoring and adaptive repair. By leveraging real-time entropy dynamics and the structural priors of reasoning trajectories, SPREG effectively detects and rectifies logical drifts before they propagate into hallucinations. Our experimental results across challenging benchmarks, such as AIME24 and AIME25, demonstrate that SPREG not only improves reasoning accuracy but also maintains high generation stability with minimal computational overhead.

The success of SPREG opens several promising avenues for future research:

  • •

    Adaptive Token-level Loss Weighting for Post-training: A natural extension of this work is to integrate the entropy signals used in SPREG directly into the model’s training phase. Traditional Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and RLHF often suffer from over-fitting due to uniform loss weighting across all tokens. Future research could explore a post-training methodology that applies differential loss weights based on token-level entropy and confidence signals Xie et al. (2025); Zhong et al. (2025). By penalizing high-uncertainty or critical reasoning tokens more heavily during optimization, we could potentially mitigate hallucination tendencies at the fundamental model level.

  • •

    Cross-Model Uncertainty Knowledge Distillation: We also aim to investigate whether the entropy patterns captured by SPREG can be distilled from larger teacher models into smaller student models. This could enable efficient, ”uncertainty-aware” small models that inherit the robust decision-making boundaries of their larger counterparts.
